title: What is the difference between UnaryOperator<T> (extends Function<T,T>) and BinaryOperator<T> (extends BiFunction<T,T,T>): they specialize for same-type input/output, used by List.replaceAll, Stream.reduce, Map.merge: and why do these specializations exist?
keyPoints: UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T>: one input, one output, same type
BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T,T,T>: two inputs, one output, all same type
They exist for type clarity: UnaryOperator signals the type does not change, avoiding redundant type parameters
UnaryOperator is used by List.replaceAll to transform each element in-place
BinaryOperator is used by Stream.reduce and Map.merge for accumulation
BinaryOperator.minBy and maxBy create operators that return the smaller or larger of two values
Both are IS-A relationships: UnaryOperator IS a Function, BinaryOperator IS a BiFunction

s1_definition.oneliner: UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T> for same-type transformations, and BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T,T,T> for same-type reductions.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **UnaryOperator<T>** – `T apply(T t)`: takes one T, returns one T. Same type in and out. Used by `List.replaceAll`.
- **BinaryOperator<T>** – `T apply(T a, T b)`: takes two T's, returns one T. All same type. Used by `Stream.reduce`, `Map.merge`.
- **Why they exist** – type clarity. Without them you would write `Function<BigDecimal, BigDecimal>` (redundant) or `BiFunction<BigDecimal, BigDecimal, BigDecimal>` (three identical types).
- **IS-A** – UnaryOperator IS a Function; BinaryOperator IS a BiFunction. They are interchangeable where the types match.
s1_definition.analogy: UnaryOperator: apply 5% interest to a balance. Takes a BigDecimal, returns a BigDecimal (same type). BinaryOperator: add two balances together. Takes two BigDecimals, returns one BigDecimal (all same type). The Operator name signals: same type in, same type out.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Type Specializations:

  Function<T, R>          UnaryOperator<T>
  T → R (different types)  T → T (same type)
  map(Trade::getAmount)    List.replaceAll(applyInterest)

  BiFunction<T, U, R>     BinaryOperator<T>
  (T, U) → R              (T, T) → T (all same type)
  Map.compute              Stream.reduce, Map.merge
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
UnaryOperator extends Function with the constraint that input and output are the same type. BinaryOperator extends BiFunction with all three types the same. They exist for API clarity: `List.replaceAll(UnaryOperator)` signals the element type does not change, and `Stream.reduce(identity, BinaryOperator)` signals all operands are the same type.

In a banking interest calculator, UnaryOperator applies 5% interest to each balance via List.replaceAll. BinaryOperator `BigDecimal::add` sums all balances via Stream.reduce and aggregates per symbol via Map.merge. BinaryOperator.minBy and maxBy create operators for comparisons.

Both are IS-A relationships: you can pass a UnaryOperator wherever Function<T,T> is expected. Use the Operator variants when types match; use plain Function/BiFunction when they differ.

Remember one sentence: UnaryOperator is Function<T,T> and BinaryOperator is BiFunction<T,T,T>, existing for type clarity when input and output are the same type.
